paper.title_en: Certified Confinement: Kernel-Checked Validation of Untrusted Quantum-Cloud Transpiler Output
paper.abstract_en: Cloud providers are adopting spatial multi-tenancy to improve quantum processing unit (QPU) utilization. However, this introduces cross-tenant vulnerabilities: otherwise hardware-legal circuits may place operations adjacent to co-tenant qubits, creating a leakage channel via physical coupling. Because tenants cannot safely trust cloud transpilers, we introduce an efficient client-side validator for buffered gate-support confinement. Given a device coupling graph, a forbidden region, and a buffer radius k, the validator rejects circuits containing non-identity gates within the forbidden zone or its k-hop neighborhood. We formally establish this structural guarantee via a Lean soundness theorem. In QASMBench experiments, we find that up to 71% of stock transpiler outputs violate this buffered policy despite being hardware-legal. Our validator catches these violations with zero false rejections when the allocation correctly reserves the buffer, yielding kernel-checked verdicts across 11 IBM device topologies. To empirically justify the buffer radius, we characterized two IBM Heron r2 QPUs. Under a 5σ distinguishing criterion, nearest-neighbor (one-hop) leakage is detectable in a median of just 186 shots, whereas two-hop leakage requires an estimated 1.3 X 105 to 1.9 X 107 shots, remaining undetectable under tested conditions. Together, our hardware measurements justify graph-buffered allocation against nearest-neighbor channels, while our formal certificate provides a rigorous guarantee of gate-support confinement.
